arxiv:2610.34735.tldr: Introduces iPrefBench, a benchmark for evaluating personal mobile-use agents on handling underspecified user tasks through history inference or direct queries.
arxiv:2610.34735.why: Too focused on mobile OS environments and end-user personal assistants to yield direct patterns for backend enterprise apps.

arxiv:2610.37666.title: ThinkWorld: World Imagination Reinforces Chain-of-Dynamics Reasoning
arxiv:2610.37666.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have made substantial progress in robotic manipulation, but their generalization remains constrained by the diversity and coverage of action-labeled robot demonstrations. Human videos provide much broader behavioral and environmental experience, while learning from them faces a fundamental trade-off between scalable data and explicit action grounding. We introduce ThinkWorld, a VLA learning framework that grounds action reasoning in world dynamics and strengthens it through reinforcement learning with world imagination. ThinkWorld represents each action thought as a Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD), a sequence of discrete motion tokens that captures the intermediate dynamics connecting the current world to a future state and serves as a common action representation across embodiments. We first initialize CoD with action-labeled demonstrations, then predict the future induced by each CoD and reinforce those whose predictions better match the observed outcome. This enables videos without action annotations to provide direct supervision from observed state transitions, allowing human and robot experience to refine the same reasoning space. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate effective human-to-robot transfer and strong generalization to unseen tasks and environments.
arxiv:2610.37666.summary_hint: ThinkWorld improves robotic generalization by representing actions as dynamics chains and using world imagination to learn from unlabeled human videos.
arxiv:2610.37666.tldr: Introduces ThinkWorld, a VLA learning framework for robotic manipulation that grounds action reasoning in world dynamics using video data.
arxiv:2610.37666.why: Irrelevant for software engineers building text/document-based LLM systems and RAG pipelines.

arxiv:2610.35193.title: Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges
arxiv:2610.35193.abstract: AI systems built around large models increasingly use experience and feedback to make persistent changes to models, prompts, memories, tools, and workflows. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) extends this process to inductive biases and to the mechanisms that govern future updates, which can themselves be revised and reused across improvement cycles. Yet self-modification alone does not guarantee trustworthy improvement. Reported gains may reflect flawed evaluations, previously acquired capabilities may deteriorate, and compliance with behavioral constraints may weaken. Compromised artifacts or sensitive information may also persist in successor systems. Changes to improvement mechanisms may invalidate earlier verification results and make human oversight less effective. This survey presents an operational definition and process framework for RSI and organizes the requirements for trustworthy RSI into four interconnected themes: genuine and sustained improvement; behavioral constraints, alignment, and fairness; system security and privacy; and transparency and controllability. We examine these themes from three perspectives: Improvement Validity, Constraint Preservation, and Effective Oversight. This analysis covers improvement diagnosis, proposal generation, proposal evaluation, and update implementation (S1--S4), including the recursive application of these stages to improvement mechanisms (RI). We review risks, safeguards, and evaluation evidence for individual updates, effects inherited by successor systems, and revisions to improvement mechanisms, while distinguishing direct RSI findings from evidence in related systems. Finally, we examine evaluation settings, identify requirements for independent and longitudinal assessment, and discuss applications and open research problems.
arxiv:2610.35193.summary_hint: This survey defines recursive self-improvement and organizes trustworthy advancement requirements into improvement validity, constraint preservation, and oversight across recursive update stages.
arxiv:2610.35193.tldr: Surveys the landscape of trustworthy recursive self-improvement in LLM-based systems, organizing requirements around genuine improvement, constraints, security, and transparency.
arxiv:2610.35193.why: Broad theoretical and safety overview; lacks immediate architectural blueprints for near-term production implementation.

arxiv:2610.34415.title: Spatial Audio Generation and Editing with Executable Plans and Self-Distilling Transfusion
arxiv:2610.34415.abstract: Spatial audio authoring coordinates source decisions with soundfield synthesis. For editing, plans specify what to change and retain, while reference audio supplies further acoustic detail. We present AMBIT, a unified framework for native First-Order Ambisonics (FOA) generation and editing with three connected contributions. First, a shared Transfusion backbone couples autoregressive planning with rectified-flow rendering through executable ScenePlans that specify source content, activity, and 3D trajectories. For editing, the plan describes the full target scene, including retained sources; contrastive features ground the requested change, while full reference latents supply residual acoustic detail for preservation. Second, an FOA-aware continuous VAE combines shared-decoder omnidirectional recovery, asymmetric grouped KL, and spatial covariance matching to preserve content and inter-channel structure. Third, joint Transfusion on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) refines planning on student-generated prefixes and rendering at sampling states reached under student plans, with target-conditioned teachers supervising both modes of the shared student. Evaluations across speech, music, and sound show improved generation content and spatial quality, acoustic fidelity during instruction-guided editing, and unedited-source preservation over the compared baselines. Project page: https://wjm-george.github.io/AMBIT/
arxiv:2610.34415.summary_hint: AMBIT is a unified framework that generates and edits first-order ambisonics audio by coupling autoregressive scene planning with rectified-flow rendering, using a specialized continuous VAE and on-policy self-distillation to preserve spatial structure and acoustic fidelity.
arxiv:2610.34415.tldr: Introduces AMBIT for spatial audio generation and editing using a shared transfusion backbone and self-distilling transfusion.
arxiv:2610.34415.why: Entirely off-topic for enterprise RAG and LLM application engineering.

arxiv:2610.34886.title: ThinkBit: Search Codewords, Recalibrate Scales, Select by Reasoning
arxiv:2610.34886.abstract: Reasoning language models generate thousands of tokens per answer, and generation speed is limited by memory bandwidth, so storing weights in two bits instead of bfloat16 can potentially make inference 8$\times$ cheaper. Two-bit methods are usually judged by perplexity and multiple-choice question-answering accuracy, both of which say little about whether a model can still reason through more difficult problems. We present ThinkBit, a strictly scalar two-bit framework built to preserve reasoning, in which every weight is an integer codeword times a bfloat16 scale shared by a group of weights. We first use a sensitivity metric to assign each layer a ternary, 2-bit, or 3-bit tier to allocate bitwidths optimally among layers. This is followed by a layerwise Gumbel-softmax-based scalar quantization algorithm that searches for optimal codewords block by block. Since a layerwise scheme does not capture how quantized layers interact with each other, we recalibrate scales, with the codewords frozen, using a knowledge-distillation-based loss against the teacher model. We then perform a short quantization-aware training (QAT) stage that lets the model mimic the base model's distribution by reassigning codewords. Finally, a paired reasoning test on training problems selects the final checkpoint between the recalibration stage and the QAT stage. On Qwen3-1.7B at matched size, our recalibrated checkpoint scores 46.7 on MATH-500 against 30.0 for EfficientQAT trained on the same data, and 73.0 after QAT on reasoning traces; at 0.52 GB it is smaller than every published 2-bit GGUF of the model yet more accurate on MATH-500. We show that this framework scales and up to 14B, a 3.74 GB model scores 94.8 on MATH-500, against 97.5 for the 29.5 GB bfloat16 model.
arxiv:2610.34886.summary_hint: ThinkBit is a scalar two-bit quantization framework that preserves reasoning by assigning layerwise bit tiers, optimizing codewords via Gumbel-softmax, and recalibrating with knowledge distillation followed by quantization-aware training.
arxiv:2610.34886.tldr: Presents ThinkBit, a strict scalar 2-bit quantization framework for reasoning LLMs that combines layerwise bitwidth allocation, Gumbel-softmax quantization, and scale recalibration.
arxiv:2610.34886.why: Relevant for reducing LLM inference costs and memory bandwidth bottlenecks when deploying large reasoning models in production.

arxiv:2610.35434.title: Skill^{infty}: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization
arxiv:2610.35434.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which a system also improves the way it improves, is a long-standing aspiration on the path to AGI. Language agents increasingly store procedural knowledge in reusable skills. Optimizing skills offers a direct way to achieve RSI, because the optimization procedure itself can be encoded as a skill. Existing skill optimizers, however, follow a hand-designed procedure. Even methods that evolve a meta-skill confine it to a fixed pipeline and relearn it for each task. We present Skill$^{\infty}$, which makes skill optimization recursively self-improving: a meta agent follows a meta-skill to optimize task skills and optimizes the meta-skill itself using the same procedure. The optimization is agent-led. The meta agent diagnoses execution traces, proposes candidates, requests independent reviews, and allocates the search budget. The meta-skill defines these steps, allowing self-improvement to rewrite them. This meta-skill is also decoupled from task skills, refined on multiple skill optimization tasks and then reused to optimize task skills across diverse domains. As in deployment, skills at both levels are standard packages loaded through native skill discovery. On 83 SkillsBench tasks, Skill$^{\infty}$ reaches a pass rate of 60.7%, compared with 56.4% for human-curated skills and 54.5% for SkillEvolver.
arxiv:2610.35434.summary_hint: Skill∞ enables recursive self-improvement by letting a meta agent optimize both task skills and its own meta-skill through a reusable, agent-led procedure, improving performance across diverse domains.
arxiv:2610.35434.tldr: Proposes Skillinfty for recursive self-improvement in language agents, using a meta agent to optimize task skills and iteratively rewrite its own meta-skill optimization procedure.
arxiv:2610.35434.why: Offers interesting ideas for advanced agent architectures and self-improving workflows, though complex to implement in standard enterprise settings.

arxiv:2610.35328.title: Constrained Decoding: Harmful or Beneficial? Revisiting Its Impact on LLM Performance
arxiv:2610.35328.abstract: Constrained decoding guarantees that Large Language Models (LLMs) produce outputs conforming to predefined formats, but is often assumed to inherently degrade reasoning. We examine this assumption through a taxonomy of three constraint types: \emph{format constraints}, which enforce output structure; \emph{validity constraints}, which mask invalid answer; and \emph{reasoning constraints}, which restrict reasoning trajectories. We theoretically show that appropriate constraints can preserve or improve performance by eliminating invalid paths. Across four model families and eleven open-source models, causal ablations on diverse benchmarks using state-of-the-art constrained decoding strategies reveal that apparent performance degradation largely stems from non-equivalent prompting and output formats rather than from decoder-level masking. Meanwhile, validity constraints improve reliability and extractability by eliminating invalid answers, while reasoning constraints can improve reasoning and, consequently, accuracy when they enforce beneficial trajectories. These findings show that the impact of constrained decoding depends on the type of constraint and the output space it removes. Our code is available.
arxiv:2610.35328.summary_hint: Constrained decoding does not inherently harm reasoning; its effects depend on constraint type, with validity and reasoning constraints often improving reliability and accuracy by removing invalid paths.
arxiv:2610.35328.tldr: Examines constrained decoding across 11 models and shows that format, validity, and reasoning constraints improve reliability and accuracy rather than degrading reasoning.
arxiv:2610.35328.why: Directly applicable for improving output reliability and enforcing structured JSON/schema generation in production LLM systems.

arxiv:2610.37375.title: Agent-Conditioned Routing: Diverse Reasoning Paths Within One Frozen Model
arxiv:2610.37375.abstract: Generating several solutions can expose alternative methods, but additional trajectories often paraphrase one dominant approach. We investigate whether the conditional capacity of a frozen sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) model can provide such diversity from one problem prompt, without user-assigned roles, prescribed methods, fine-tuning, or model copies. Agent-Conditioned Routing (ACR) assigns $m$ parallel trajectories persistent, untrained shared/private expert-eligibility masks while preserving the learned, input-dependent token router. On a screened 126-question multi-mode mathematics and physics benchmark, with model judges reading the reported derivations in full, we count the number of problems yielding at least two distinct primary methods among soft-correct solutions in four trajectories. ACR reaches approximately twice as many such problems as the strongest temperature setting under GLM 5.3 (37.3 versus 18.7), and 1.67 times as many under GPT-5.6 Sol (45.00 versus 27.00), at matched output budgets. A blinded four-expert audit on a stratified sample of 30 problems also finds more multi-method solutions with ACR on both backbones, with lower correctness. Matched-eligibility ablations show modest multi-method count advantages for ACR, while token-resampled masks attain higher correctness. An informed sequential prompt elicits more diversity still, using previous solutions and explicit requests for alternative methods. ACR adds about 160 KiB of mask state. In a three-problem microbenchmark capped at 1,024 tokens, its latency and peak VRAM usage remain within 3% of batched temperature sampling.
arxiv:2610.37375.tldr: Introduces Agent-Conditioned Routing (ACR), assigning persistent expert-eligibility masks to parallel trajectories in a frozen MoE model to generate diverse reasoning paths.
arxiv:2610.37375.why: Provides a method to elicit diverse reasoning paths from a single frozen model without extra fine-tuning or model copies.

arxiv:2610.37080.title: Tessera: Structure-Completed Evidence Units for Web Retrieval-Augmented Generation
arxiv:2610.37080.abstract: Web retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) splits a page into fixed-size text chunks or, in recent visual pipelines, screenshot tiles, and the retrieved item serves at once as the unit of indexing, ranking, and reading. We trace answer evidence from source HTML to reader input over the full English Wikipedia and find that this coupling loses evidence in text and screenshot pipelines alike: evidence present in the source page often fails to reach the reader intact, particularly structured content such as tables and infoboxes, which chunking separates from the headers and context that give it meaning. Stronger extraction, context expansion, and larger reader budgets leave the loss in place. We present Tessera, a training-free evidence delivery layer that decouples what a pipeline retrieves from what its reader reads. Given the pages behind any ranked list, Tessera rebuilds their HTML into fine-grained evidence units, each completed with its page title, section path, and table headers, selects the units relevant to the query, and packs them into the reader context at an unchanged token budget. The index, the retriever, and the reader stay as they are, so Tessera applies to text, screenshot, and agentic pipelines. Across three question answering benchmarks, Tessera improves answer accuracy by 5 to 6 points on text and screenshot pipelines, consistently across readers, retrievers, and reader budgets, and outperforms strong HTML-aware and structure-aware RAG baselines under matched budgets. The gains carry over to multi-step agentic search. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/sarendis56/Tessera.
arxiv:2610.37080.tldr: Presents Tessera, a training-free evidence delivery layer that rebuilds raw HTML into fine-grained units with section paths and table headers, decoupling retrieval from reading.
arxiv:2610.37080.why: Directly applicable drop-in improvement for web RAG and document parsing pipelines that struggle with tables and structured content separation.

arxiv:2610.36991.title: SpectRAG: Weighted Chunk Graphs for Token-Budgeted Context Selection in Multi-Hop Retrieval-Augmented Generation
arxiv:2610.36991.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems ground large language models (LLMs) by retrieving external evidence and conditioning generation on the retrieved context. Although dense retrieval is effective for local semantic matching, independently ranked retrieval can return redundant passages, miss cross-chunk dependencies, and provide incomplete evidence for multi-hop reasoning. We propose SpectRAG, a spectral graph-augmented retrieval framework that combines hybrid candidate seeding, weighted chunk graph construction, graph-based expansion, spectral relevance propagation, and token-budgeted context selection. Document chunks are represented by dense semantic embeddings and graph-spectral coordinates derived from a weighted chunk graph whose edges encode semantic similarity, document adjacency, section hierarchy, shared entities, citation links, and similarity between LLM-generated utility questions. At query time, SpectRAG builds a high-recall seed set using exact inner-product search and hybrid relevance signals, expands it over the chunk graph, re-scores candidates using graph proximity and spectral information, and assembles the final context under a fixed token budget. The goal is not merely to retrieve individually similar chunks, but to construct a context that is relevant, diverse, structurally connected, and sufficient for grounded reasoning. Experiments on MultiHopRAG, UltraDomain, and long-document question-answering settings show that SpectRAG improves broad evidence recovery and achieves competitive generation quality against dense, hybrid, HyDE, LightRAG, and NaiveRAG baselines. The results further indicate that graph-spectral structure is particularly useful for inference-oriented and cross-document retrieval, while highlighting trade-offs in early precision, computational cost, and domain-dependent performance.
arxiv:2610.36991.tldr: Proposes SpectRAG, a spectral graph-augmented retrieval framework combining weighted chunk graphs, semantic similarity, and spectral relevance propagation for multi-hop RAG.
arxiv:2610.36991.why: Provides a concrete graph-based retrieval strategy to handle multi-hop dependencies and reduce context redundancy in enterprise search.

arxiv:2610.36890.title: Latent Residual Reasoning for Ranking in Generative Recommendation
arxiv:2610.36890.abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) models for ranking typically adopt a fast-thinking direct prediction paradigm with strong practical efficiency. However, ranking requires fine-grained scoring across multiple candidate items, while existing GR models still mainly rely on one-shot prediction. This raises the question whether additional inference-time computation can further improve ranking quality. Recently, inspired by Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning in large language models (LLMs), some work has begun to introduce reasoning into recommendation systems. Some of these methods rely on LLM reasoning frameworks to perform explicit reasoning in textual space, but such designs are not suitable for more widely deployed non-textual recommendation models. A more relevant direction is to introduce latent reasoning into ID-based recommendation models. Although recent work has extended latent reasoning to industrial ranking, how successive reasoning steps should improve fine-grained candidate scores remains less explored. To address this problem, we propose Refiner, a latent residual reasoning framework with parameter-efficient fine-tuning for generative ranking. Our approach introduces three key components: (1) a residual reasoning mechanism that progressively refines ranking scores through cumulative additive corrections, (2) history queries that provide condensed user behavior representations to enhance candidate-specific reasoning, and (3) a parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategy that leverages LoRA modules to adapt pre-trained models for latent reasoning. Extensive experiments on two public benchmarks, an offline industrial dataset, and an online A/B test demonstrate that Refiner consistently improves over direct prediction, validating its effectiveness and practical utility.
arxiv:2610.36890.tldr: Proposes Refiner, a latent residual reasoning framework for ID-based generative recommendation systems.
arxiv:2610.36890.why: Narrowly focused on recommendation systems rather than general LLM apps, RAG, or agent orchestration.

arxiv:2610.36561.title: Governed Sovereign RAG for Public Administration: Tripartite Epistemic Routing, Facet-Guided Clarification, and Deterministic Numeric Verification in Citizen Services
arxiv:2610.36561.abstract: Deploying conversational assistants at government service desks faces a tension between regulatory certainty (zero tolerance for invented fees), data sovereignty prohibiting commercial clouds, and high rates of underspecified or out-of-jurisdiction citizen queries. We present and evaluate a governed, sovereign Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture deployed on the official portal of the State of Tlaxcala, Mexico (tlaxcaladigital.gob.mx), covering 1,143 procedures and a decoupled directory of 924 offices. The system governs interactions via three pillars: (1) a two-stage tripartite epistemic gate (clarify_policy and a Boltzmann distribution over AnyJev) arbitrating among answering (SPECIFIC), facet-guided clarification (CLARIFY), and abstaining (ABSTAIN); (2) a post-generation deterministic numeric verifier (verify_numeric_guardrail) with SHA-256 cache invalidation ensuring every generated fee or validity figure belongs to the retrieved official record; and (3) an empirical evaluation across 380 organic production traces (8 weeks) and a 200-query stratified benchmark (5-fold CV: 86.41% +/- 7.50%). In production, 89.47% of traffic is resolved at Level 0 via deterministic templates without free generation (global p50 = 0.665 s; direct L0 p50 = 0.445 s; slow-tail p95 = 30.412 s under CPU queuing), with 0/40 fiscal amount hallucinations observed in Level 1 (95% bound <= 8.81%). On the benchmark, the system achieves 86.50% strict Top-1 accuracy (+10.00 pp over a binary neural gate, p = 0.00453, p_Holm = 0.01172), pairing a 93.00% conditional safe upper bound with a 70.87% dropout-adjusted effective resolution after accounting for 53.33% citizen drop-off in clarification menus.
arxiv:2610.36561.tldr: Evaluates a governed sovereign RAG architecture featuring a tripartite epistemic routing gate and a post-generation deterministic numeric verifier for citizen services.
arxiv:2610.36561.why: Valuable patterns for high-stakes enterprise RAG applications requiring strict hallucination guards and deterministic verification of numeric data.

arxiv:2610.35592.title: GEAR: Feature-Based Configuration and Code Generation for Agentic Systems
arxiv:2610.35592.abstract: Engineering multi-agent systems (MAS) requires choosing agents, orchestration strategies, communication mechanisms, reasoning approaches, and memory configurations. These choices depend on framework-specific capabilities and abstractions, requiring developers to learn different APIs when exploring alternative implementations. We present GEAR, an open-source tool for configuring MAS and generating framework-specific implementations from a common specification. GEAR uses a feature-based representation to make configuration options and their constraints explicit, enabling users to validate specifications before code generation. Through connectors for ten agentic frameworks, users generate projects from the same specification and can then inspect reports describing framework-specific adaptations. A preliminary assessment of mapping feasibility identifies translation strategies for 271 of 320 evaluated feature-framework pairs (84.69%). GEAR supports developers prototyping agentic systems and researchers exploring MAS configurations across frameworks. GEAR is available as open-source software at https://github.com/brellsanwouo/gear-framework and a video demo is available at https://youtu.be/iwNi-oC2tCw.
arxiv:2610.35592.tldr: Introduces GEAR, a tool that uses feature-based representations to configure multi-agent systems and generate framework-specific code for 10 different agentic frameworks.
arxiv:2610.35592.why: Useful prototyping utility when evaluating multiple agent frameworks and standardizing agent configuration specifications.

arxiv:2610.34673.title: Agent Memory as Recommendation: Recommender-System Design for Long-Term Memory of LLM Agents
arxiv:2610.34673.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents that serve users across many sessions must choose, for every request, the few stored memories that enter a limited context window. This choice largely decides whether the agent answers correctly, and it runs on every request at Web scale. This selection faces three challenges: a large and growing store, a per-request cost budget, and multi-session questions that need all of their evidence. Many memory systems build notes or graphs with hundreds to thousands of LLM calls per history, and each is designed on its own, so it is unclear which component yields the accuracy. These challenges mirror the properties of recommendation, so we formalize agent memory as budgeted slate recommendation, with the request as the user, stored memories as items and the context window as a slate. The formalization places memory systems in one design space of recommender cascades and factorizes accuracy into the completeness that each stage controls. Guided by it, we propose AgentMemRec, which adapts candidate generation, learning to rank and slate construction from recommender systems and selects memories without any LLM call. On multi-session questions of LongMemEval, AgentMemRec outperforms memory and context-selection methods, including A-Mem, HippoRAG 2, DynamicRAG and T-Mem, by 10 to 31 points of accuracy. It matches an LLM reranker that makes 64 calls per query at 3.2 times lower serving cost, and on LoCoMo it outperforms Mem0 and Zep without any LLM call at write time. The factorization attributes the gains to slates that more often hold all of the evidence, so recommender-system design offers an effective and efficient foundation for the long-term memory of LLM agents.
arxiv:2610.34673.tldr: They formalized LLM agent long-term memory retrieval as budgeted slate recommendation, introducing AgentMemRec to handle candidate generation, learning-to-rank, and slate construction within per-request cost budgets.
arxiv:2610.34673.why: Directly applicable to improving retrieval, context windows, and cost efficiency in long-running production agent systems.

arxiv:2610.35966.title: EMMA: Structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent Workflow Synthesis
arxiv:2610.35966.abstract: Deploying LLM agents in specialized domains often require fine-grained task-specific procedures and knowledge a general model lacks, yet parameter training is costly and non-interpretable, and hand-engineered agent systems shift the cost to expert labor. Episodic memory updates at context level, but single agent adaptation struggles to alleviate cross-task interference, especially with complex tasks such as multi-application navigation or data pool analysis. Although multi-agent evolution alleviates this problem, existing methods lack clear definitions on update rules and rely on the backbone model to decide where and how much the system changes. This ill-scoped evolution makes learning follow the backbone's structural preferences rather than the observed failures: one backbone accumulates skills while another spawns agents. We present EMMA (structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent workflow synthesis), which treats the configuration of a multi-agent system (controller routing memory, specialists inheriting a generalist prompt, and per-step procedural skills) as episodic memory. EMMA makes the ownership and admissibility of updates explicit: a reflector assigns each diagnosed failure to the scope owning its correction and proposes one edit within it, and backbone-independent guards keep every accepted edit scoped, incremental and bounded. Across KramaBench, AppWorld and BBEH with five backbones and four baselines (ACE, GEPA, EvoMAS and ADAS), EMMA attains the best overall performance on every benchmark, up to 32.5% over the strongest baseline, maintains consistent improvements across backbones, and uses 17-38% fewer training executions than the most efficient baseline.
arxiv:2610.35966.tldr: They introduced EMMA, treating multi-agent system configurations—including controller routing and procedural skills—as structured episodic memory to avoid cross-task interference without expensive parameter training.
arxiv:2610.35966.why: Provides concrete architectural patterns for organizing reliable, multi-agent workflows and managing state across sessions.

arxiv:2610.33503.title: Novel or Not? PatEx-Gym: Agentic Prior-Art Search for Novelty Assessment in Patent Examination
arxiv:2610.33503.abstract: Patent examination is a challenging real-world task that requires agents to discover sparse prior art, iteratively refine queries, inspect technical evidence, and produce novelty assessments documented in Office Actions (OAs) across heterogeneous scientific and technical domains. However, existing benchmarks largely focus on static and limited candidate sets, leaving the full search--reasoning--assessment process underexplored. We present PatEx-Gym, the first framework for developing and evaluating agents for patent examination, which integrates three components. First, PatEx-Bench provides 1K realistic examination tasks, two large-scale retrieval corpora containing over 1M patents and 52K scientific papers, and a harness runtime supporting iterative search, document visits, reasoning, and OA generation. Second, we introduce PASS, an annotation-free Prior-Art Agentic Search Trajectory Synthesis framework. Specifically, it exploits document visits as implicit relevance signals and evidence-acquisition anchors to model intra-turn query behavior, inter-turn search progression, and trajectory-level evidence and outcome quality, yielding PatEx-SynData. Third, we train PatEx-Agent at the 4B scale via supervised fine-tuning on the curated trajectories, establishing a lightweight baseline. Extensive experiments show that final decision accuracy alone does not fully reflect examination quality, while prior-art discovery remains difficult even for strong frontier models. Our PatEx-Agent achieves competitive performance against substantially larger general-purpose agents. These results show that training on PatEx-SynData enables a compact 4B model to serve as a competitive baseline for prior-art search and patent examination. We view patent examination as a demanding testbed for agentic search and deep research agents.
arxiv:2610.33503.tldr: They built PatEx-Gym, a benchmark and framework for agentic prior-art search in patent examination, along with an annotation-free trajectory synthesis method using document visits as implicit relevance signals.
arxiv:2610.33503.why: Narrow domain application (patent examination), though the trajectory synthesis and iterative search methods offer interesting background for complex RAG loops.

arxiv:2610.36980.title: AutoVend: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Autonomous Vending Operations
arxiv:2610.36980.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are extending agent-mediated commerce on the Web from shopping for consumers to operating businesses for sellers. In online-to-offline (O2O) commerce, decisions are issued through Web-based platforms but realized through costly physical execution. Evaluating such agents requires going beyond individual transactions to ask whether decisions made online turn into sustained economic returns. We introduce AutoVend, a benchmark in which one LLM agent manages 20 vending machines across five site types through a Web-based operating interface for 180 simulated days. Its data-grounded simulator combines a shared warehouse, procurement lead times, paid replenishment, inventory expiration, and recurring operating costs. We evaluate five LLM agents against a rule-based inventory-control baseline and diagnose their site coordination, execution, and performance over time. Four of five evaluated LLM agents fall short of this baseline, and returns per dollar of inference cost rank models differently from returns alone. Operational analyses show that gains in individual metrics do not consistently yield stronger economic growth, as inventory and execution costs erode these gains. Trajectory analysis further reveals difficulties in grounding feasible actions, managing inventory commitments, and converting feedback into effective policy revisions.
arxiv:2610.36980.tldr: They introduced AutoVend, a long-horizon benchmark evaluating LLM agents on online-to-offline vending machine operations over 180 simulated days, showing that most models underperform rule-based baselines.
arxiv:2610.36980.why: Useful evaluation methodology for long-horizon agent loops, but focused on commerce operations rather than core enterprise search or RAG.

arxiv:2610.35142.title: CalibraRL: Confidence-Calibrated Reinforcement Learning for Mitigating Hallucinations in RAG
arxiv:2610.35142.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often produce plausible but incorrect answers, motivating reinforcement learning methods that reward correct answers, penalize incorrect answers, and allow abstention. However, fixed outcome-based rewards do not distinguish incorrect responses with different confidence levels or account for differences in answering reliability across queries. Consequently, such rewards may inadequately penalize overconfident errors and fail to discourage unnecessary abstention. We propose CalibraRL, a reinforcement learning framework that incorporates response confidence and query-level answering evidence into reward design. For non-abstaining responses, CalibraRL combines correctness-based utility with a Brier-based penalty that encourages agreement between confidence and correctness. For abstentions, it estimates conditional answering reliability using a Beta posterior derived from the correctness of non-abstaining responses within each sampled group. The abstention reward increases with the posterior probability that the model's accuracy on non-abstaining responses is below a predefined threshold. CalibraRL reuses training rollouts without requiring additional annotations indicating whether the model knows the answer to each question. Experiments on three QA datasets demonstrate that CalibraRL improves answer precision and reduces hallucinations compared with strong baselines. Further analysis shows that CalibraRL reduces mean expected calibration error (ECE) by 30.8\% across two backbone models and three datasets, highlighting its potential to improve the reliability of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in web search.
arxiv:2610.35142.tldr: They proposed CalibraRL, a reinforcement learning framework combining correctness utility with a Brier-based confidence penalty and Beta posterior abstention rewards to mitigate hallucinations in RAG.
arxiv:2610.35142.why: Directly tackles hallucination reduction, confidence calibration, and reliable abstention logic for production RAG pipelines.

arxiv:2610.34860.title: Semantic Atoms for Scalable Text Analysis in Data Analytics in the Era of LLM-Based Agents
arxiv:2610.34860.abstract: Much of the information needed for data analysis is buried in text columns: an analyst may infer customer frustration from complaint text and use it to explain resolution time. We call workloads in which processing text columns is central to subsequent data analysis TADA (\emph{Text Analysis in Data Analytics}). In an agentic setting, the user's query dynamically specifies this processing, and answering it interleaves LLM-based semantic steps with exact SQL or Python operations. This mixed execution raises two design questions: which work should be neural and which symbolic, and which semantic outputs later steps can reuse. We address them for agent-planned TADA workflows with two complementary, query-driven semantic atoms. Each atom takes a sequence of text items and a natural-language query specifying the semantic task: \textbf{Tagging} returns one string per input item, while \textbf{Categorization} returns $M$ category objects over $N$ input items. Tagging results are materialized as a row-aligned column and Categorization results as a category table; SQL or Python then performs exact computation over this exposed state. We realize this interface in TADA-Agent, whose atoms run inside generated Python programs and internally handle inputs beyond a reliable context window. We evaluate TADA-Agent on TABench, a benchmark of 40 complete analysis requests over spreadsheet tables spanning workflow composition, input--output structure, and literature-grounded analytical scenarios. Against a semantic-operator baseline and relative to a held-out TADA reference run, TADA-Agent delivers comparable row-level semantic quality, has higher complete-artifact preservation estimates, and uses over an order of magnitude fewer semantic-model requests under the evaluated native execution paths.
arxiv:2610.34860.tldr: They defined Tagging and Categorization semantic atoms for LLM-based text analysis in data workflows, interleaving neural text steps with exact SQL or Python operations.
arxiv:2610.34860.why: Offers architectural patterns for mixing LLM text extraction with structured SQL/Python data pipelines in enterprise applications.

arxiv:2610.34653.title: Heard Enough to Act: Early Tool Calling in Spoken Dialogue Systems
arxiv:2610.34653.abstract: Latency-sensitive spoken agents must know not only which tool to call, but also when they have heard enough to act. Waiting for the turn to complete delays execution even when the request is already actionable. However, neither existing spoken agents nor spoken dialogue corpora define the earliest point at which a request becomes actionable. We introduce a synthetic spoken-dialogue pipeline that provides earliest-actionable-point supervision, marking when the observed speech grounds a tool and its required arguments. Through controlled task generation, speech synthesis and alignment, and gated annotation, we construct 26,694 dialogues totaling 786 hours across 48 domains, with disjoint training and test argument values. We additionally create an audio rendering of $τ^2$-bench for external evaluation. We train an omni-modal language model on this corpus, enabling causal, chunk-level decisions and partial-transcript generation for downstream call completion. The model achieves tool-state macro-F1 scores of 0.48 and 0.47 on held-out dialogues and the external benchmark, respectively. For correct calls, the estimated mean lead over a turn-end cascade, using the same formatter, is 1.8-2.0 seconds in-domain and 1.1 seconds on $τ^2$-bench. These results demonstrate a data-driven path toward spoken agents that act while listening. We will open-source the pipeline and the training scripts.
arxiv:2610.34653.tldr: They constructed a synthetic spoken-dialogue corpus with earliest-actionable-point supervision and trained a model for causal, chunk-level tool calling and partial transcript generation.
arxiv:2610.34653.why: Interesting techniques for reducing latency via early tool invocation, though specifically tailored for real-time spoken dialogue systems.

arxiv:2610.37471.title: PerceptRL: Making Visual Perception Rewardable in MLLMs from Answers to Interactions
arxiv:2610.37471.abstract: Fine-grained visual perception remains a bottleneck during post-training of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), as perceptual errors can constrain gains from reasoning-focused optimization. Although image-caption pre-training improves perception, its influence can weaken as subsequent stages change data mixtures and objectives. Continuing caption supervision during post-training is challenging because subjective, information-dense descriptions complicate verifiable reward design. We present PerceptRL, which strengthens perception at two complementary levels. Perception RL uses a multi-agent pipeline to extract verified errors from dense image captions and convert the corresponding visual facts into QA pairs with fixed answer labels and rule-based rewards. Chain QA links correlated errors, while multiple-choice QA combines unrelated errors. A specialized route targets high-error domains with tailored verification, and a domain-agnostic general route covers errors beyond these domains. Perception Agentic RL addresses fine-grained and dense cases unresolved by single-turn Perception RL through multi-turn inspection with visual tools. We observe coordinate drift even in models trained to use tools, where incorrect crops or annotations distort evidence and propagate errors. Coordinate Injection corrects spatial operations in cold-start trajectories, while a grounding-aware process reward supervises intermediate spatial fidelity alongside final-answer correctness. Training proceeds through shared cold-start SFT, single-turn Perception RL, and multi-turn Perception Agentic RL. Across seven benchmarks under a shared tool-use protocol, PerceptRL achieves 71.6% average accuracy, surpassing the base model with the same tools and the strongest evaluated frontier VLM by 15.7 and 5.2 percentage points, respectively.
arxiv:2610.37471.tldr: They introduced PerceptRL to improve multimodal LLM visual perception by extracting verified errors from image captions into QA pairs with rule-based rewards.
arxiv:2610.37471.why: Too focused on multimodal visual perception and MLLM post-training rather than standard text-based RAG or agent orchestration.

arxiv:2610.37195.title: Action-Value Calibration via Continuation Sharing for Long-Horizon Agentic Reinforcement Learning
arxiv:2610.37195.abstract: Reinforcement learning for long-horizon agents relies on feedback from sequences of interactions, making credit assignment to individual actions difficult. Existing methods such as GiGPO compare actions at shared states to compute relative advantages, but estimate each action's value from a single sampled continuation. The resulting local credit remains sensitive to decisions made later in the trajectory. To address this problem, we propose ConCal (Continuation Calibration), a recursive continuation-value estimator that incorporates continuation evidence already present in a rollout batch. ConCal matches visits from the same task by their incoming state-action-state transitions, combines shared continuation evidence with each visit's own transition estimate, and propagates calibrated values backward to refine earlier action-value estimates. This reduces dependence on individual sampled continuations and mitigates local credit distortions without additional rollouts. Held-out return diagnostics show lower error in within-group value differences and higher agreement with reference action orderings than estimates based on individual continuations. With Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, ConCal improves success rates over GiGPO by 3.39 and 5.86 percentage points on ALFWorld and WebShop, respectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/Yingjian-Chen/ConCal.
arxiv:2610.37195.tldr: They proposed ConCal, a recursive continuation-value estimator for long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning that matches transition visits to share evidence and reduce local credit assignment error.
arxiv:2610.37195.why: Provides methodological improvements for credit assignment in multi-step agent trajectories, useful if training proprietary agent policies.

arxiv:2610.36848.title: Evolving Agent Teams
arxiv:2610.36848.abstract: The rapid progress of software engineering agents drives interest in applying them to open-ended problems such as GPU kernel optimization. However, we find that existing coding agents converge to local optima on real-world, expert-written kernels (e.g., FlashInfer). We introduce Evolving Agent Teams, a multi-agent framework that escapes such local optima. It features (1) a central supervisor that diagnoses each local optimum and restructures a team of agents; and (2) a persistent file system that comprises a learning document, an evolution history, and per-team artifacts, grounding restructuring with accumulated experience. Under a matched token budget, Evolving Agent Teams consistently outperforms strong coding-agent baselines. With an extended token budget, Evolving Agent Teams generates a CUDA kernel that reaches 1.2x mean speedup over the production FlashInfer MLA paged decode kernel from scratch and wins on 36 of 47 production workloads from FlashInfer-Bench (0.86-0.99x on the remaining 11). It also demonstrates superior performance on tasks such as KDA prefill on AMD MI350X (3.01x over vLLM) and NVIDIA B200 (3.44x over FlashKDA), MoE expert-offload serving on Apple silicon (30.3 tokens/s decode for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in MLX 4-bit on a 48 GB M4 Pro), and RoboDojo robot manipulation (62.1 on held-out seeds vs. 55.3 for the best leaderboard entry). Code is available at https://github.com/caoshiyi/EAT.
arxiv:2610.36848.tldr: They developed Evolving Agent Teams, using a central supervisor to restructure coding agent teams and a persistent file system based on accumulated experience to escape local optima.
arxiv:2610.36848.why: Useful multi-agent orchestration pattern for complex tasks, though demonstrated primarily on software engineering and GPU kernel optimization.

arxiv:2610.36589.title: InfraDev: Can Coding Agents Develop AI Infrastructure, and How Can We Tell?
arxiv:2610.36589.abstract: Coding agents are beginning to develop the production-grade AI infrastructure that trains and serves large models, yet existing benchmarks cover only single kernels or single-GPU tasks, and grade with tests and prompts that misjudge both correct and incorrect patches. We introduce InfraDev, a benchmark of 36 tasks built from real-world pull requests to Megatron-LM, vLLM, and verl, covering infrastructure development for training, inference, and reinforcement learning. Each task asks an agent to reimplement a real change that spans many files and must run correctly across many GPUs. To grade such changes, we jointly synthesize hidden probes, which enforce the requirements the original tests leave unchecked, and a prompt that states every interface the probes call without revealing the solution. We also design a shared execution environment that reuses dependencies and artifacts across tasks, cutting storage by 52-57% and build time by 13-14% on Megatron-LM and vLLM. Across six frontier models, the best resolves only 38.9% of the tasks; the probes reject 32% of the submissions that pass every official test, and with the original pull request descriptions as prompts, no model resolves a single task. Failure analysis shows that structural and state errors dominate and that agents' own tests rarely check memory, time, or traffic. Turning these findings into an agent skill raises the resolved rate of a frontier model on the Megatron-LM tasks by 10.5%.
arxiv:2610.36589.tldr: InfraDev presents 36 multi‑file pull‑request tasks for coding agents to modify AI infrastructure code across GPUs; hidden probes catch missing requirements. Top model solves 38.9% of tasks, with probes rejecting 32% of apparently passing submissions.
arxiv:2610.36589.why: Helps evaluate and improve coding agents that could automate infra changes in your LLM deployment pipelines.

arxiv:2610.36254.title: Instant Software Factories
arxiv:2610.36254.abstract: Coding agents can quickly build prototypes, but a long tail of fixes, optimizations, tests, and releases separates a prototype from a product. A software factory handles this ongoing work through a repeatable process. We ask whether this work needs dedicated orchestration and how such factories should be judged. Given a tested repository and a coding agent, an instant software factory uses only two coordination inputs, a swarm of cron-job agents with standing objectives and a shared communication board, such as GitHub, where agents coordinate through the traces they leave. We developed a bootstrap prompt designed to set up both inputs from one round of human input, with governance as a separable layer. We distilled it from two manually configured industrial factories, observed for 15 and 17 days, and have not yet evaluated it. In the GitHub-coordinated CLI factory, daily merges rose 15x during agent rollout, an observed association. Its agents also filed 95% of new issues and authored 40 of 58 PRs that changed CI workflows, and at least 5.6% of issues marked as fixed were later found to have incorrect fixes. Unlike an agent scored on a fixed benchmark, a factory thus changes its own workload, evaluator, and measured progress. We formulate factory development as multi-objective optimization under this endogenous feedback. Over five months, we plan to evolve both factories, test the bootstrap on new repositories, and test five falsifiable hypotheses.
arxiv:2610.36254.tldr: Instant Software Factory uses a swarm of cron‑job agents coordinated via a shared GitHub board to turn coding agents into repeatable production pipelines; observed 15‑x merge rate increase and agents filed 95% of new issues.
arxiv:2610.36254.why: Provides a low‑overhead pattern for scaling agent‑driven code updates in your cloud services.

arxiv:2610.34577.title: Rethinking Verification in Agent Harnesses
arxiv:2610.34577.abstract: Agent harnesses enable large language models to act through tools, observe the results, and iteratively work toward a task goal. Verification checks and revises agents' work to improve output quality. Yet there is limited guidance on how harnesses should organize this effort. We study verification as an axis of test-time scaling by examining when to intervene, who checks the work, and how checking leads to revision. Our framework spans four layers of the agent lifecycle: initial instructions, mid-turn reminders, completion gates, and independent review. We compare 17 designs across seven frontier coding models on Terminal-Bench (TB) and SWE-bench Verified (SWE), and introduce VisualBench for expert evaluation of visual and interactive artifacts. Initial instructions and execution-time reminders yield modest, model-dependent average gains on the coding benchmarks, without substantially increasing average output token use. Completion gates can yield larger gains but may substantially increase cost. Independent review by a critic offers a more favorable accuracy-cost tradeoff, improving average accuracy by 5.9-9.5 percentage points on TB and 3.9-6.6 on SWE at 1.13-1.25 and 1.00-1.04 times baseline cost, respectively. On VisualBench, independent review achieves net preferences of 13.2-23.8 points over the baseline across its four designs, exceeding the evaluated L0-L2 designs. Additional review rounds or independent critics further improve average TB accuracy by up to 3.5 percentage points. Together, these results provide empirical guidance for verification design in agent harnesses and support independent review as a practical axis of test-time scaling.
arxiv:2610.34577.summary_hint: Verification strategies for agent harnesses—spanning instructions, reminders, gates, and independent review—show that independent critic review improves accuracy with minimal cost increases, guiding practical test-time scaling design.
arxiv:2610.34577.tldr: Analyzes 17 verification designs across four harness layers (instructions, reminders, gates, critics) for coding agents; independent critic review gives best accuracy‑cost trade‑off, modest gains from prompts and reminders, larger gains but higher cost from completion gates.
arxiv:2610.34577.why: Guides adding cheap verification steps to improve reliability of your RAG agents without large latency.

arxiv:2610.34634.title: AgentProofBench: Benchmarking Reusable Verifiers for Web Agents
arxiv:2610.34634.abstract: Reusable Web-agent verification requires a rule to follow changing requirements and support subsequent execution. We introduce AgentProofBench, which connects paired tests of a frozen acceptance rule to execution from identical saved openings. The resource spans 97 tasks, 79 families, and four Web services. Experiments with DeepSeek Flash/Pro establish two linked measurements. Across 48 families, complete-panel and decision-replay tests retain 82/96 Flash and 79/96 Pro source programs; paired reuse-rebuild BA intervals are [-5.47, 1.57] and [-10.16, 0.00] percentage points. Across 22 execution families, deployment-state panel correctness separates program assignments whose two saved openings are both delivered correctly: 32/33 assignments with error-free panels, versus 1/11 with panel errors. All reference-defined program-gate regressions and withheld deliveries occur in the latter group. Neutral continuation attains the highest correct delivery under the tested generic feedback, providing a concrete baseline for measuring the value added by a gate. Released instructions, states, programs, reference rules, and trajectories connect each test failure to its execution consequences. AgentProofBench makes reusable verification assessable at both the requirement and policy levels.
arxiv:2610.34634.summary_hint: AgentProofBench evaluates reusable web-agent verification by linking frozen acceptance rules to execution traces, establishing baseline measurements for program-gate correctness and reuse.
arxiv:2610.34634.tldr: AgentProofBench provides 97 web‑agent tasks with paired acceptance‑rule tests and saved execution states; measures reuse of verifiers across families, showing Flash retains 82% and Pro 79% of source programs.
arxiv:2610.34634.why: Helps assess how well your agent verification logic generalizes across similar web tasks.

arxiv:2610.36456.title: LociArt: A Unified Paradigm for Free-Style Local Video Stylization
arxiv:2610.36456.abstract: Video stylization typically transforms entire scenes, while local artistic editing requires precise region--style association, spatial control, and temporal consistency. We introduce LociArt, a unified paradigm for free-style local video stylization that explicitly specifies where to stylize and what style to apply while preserving non-target content. At its core, GRNStyle builds on Generative Refinement Networks (GRN) and introduces a polar style-aware mask that embeds style identities as equal-norm directions within selected regions. Complementary representation--geometry conditioning combines encoded mask features with raw-mask spatial support, integrating spatiotemporal context with geometric control. To provide paired supervision, we develop an automated pipeline combining global stylization, video object removal, matting, and compositing, and construct the LociArt-100K Dataset with 100K local stylization pairs. We further establish the LociArt Benchmark, comprising 80 source videos and 84 target masks covering 168 foreground/background stylization cases, with a Style Prototype Similarity (SPS) evaluation scheme for regional style quality and complementary measures of non-target preservation and temporal consistency. Experiments show that GRNStyle outperforms existing methods in regional style quality and spatial control while maintaining strong temporal consistency. Qualitative examples further illustrate joint stylization of multiple regions with the same or different learned styles, despite training only on single-region, single-style pairs. Together, these components provide a unified foundation for learning and evaluating controllable local video stylization. Project page: https://higherhu.github.io/lociart/.
arxiv:2610.36456.summary_hint: LociArt enables precise local video stylization with region-style control and temporal consistency via a generative refinement network, automated dataset construction, and a dedicated benchmark.
arxiv:2610.36456.tldr: LociArt introduces a method for local video stylization using polar style‑aware masks and geometry conditioning, with a 100K paired dataset and benchmark.
arxiv:2610.36456.why: Focuses on video art; unrelated to LLM retrieval or agents.

arxiv:2610.35439.title: Omni-InteractScope: Benchmarking Proactive and Agentic Interaction in Continuous Omnimodal Streams
arxiv:2610.35439.abstract: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) are increasingly expected to assist users while observing continuous audiovisual streams. However, existing evaluations provide limited insight into how reliably these models connect stream evidence and user needs to timely, sustained interventions. We introduce Omni-InteractScope, a benchmark of 1,479 human-annotated, cross-reviewed interactions with 1,790 temporal targets across eight task groups. It links input modalities, event triggers, intervention types, and user needs, covering event-timed tool invocation and query-free assistance alongside notifications, warnings, state tracking, and continuous responses. Our experimental results on the proposed benchmark reveal three critical limitations of current Omni-LLMs: (1) Timely tool invocation remains unreliable: all 12 evaluated models produce an on-time first response for at most 40\% of tool-invocation targets, and joint timing-and-tool accuracy reaches at most 32.0\%. (2) Query-free reminders remain poorly covered: all evaluated models achieve lower timely reference-target recall on query-free reminders than on explicit questions, measured on their respective target sets. Reminder recall never exceeds 23.0\%. (3) End-to-end guidance coverage remains limited: nine models cover none of the 26 guidance sequences in full, and the remaining three cover only one to three sequences each. Targeted controls further show that tool-invocation scores alone do not establish event grounding and that reminder coverage depends on response history and frequency. These findings motivate developing and evaluating streaming assistants for timely action, initiative under general user needs, and coverage of entire response sequences.
arxiv:2610.35439.summary_hint: Omni-InteractScope evaluates continuous audiovisual interaction reliability, revealing that current Omni-LLMs struggle with timely tool use, query-free reminders, and sustained guidance.
arxiv:2610.35439.tldr: Omni-InteractScope benchmark contains 1,479 annotated interactions over continuous audiovisual streams; shows current Omni‑LLMs achieve ≤40% on‑time tool invocation and ≤32% joint timing‑tool accuracy.
arxiv:2610.35439.why: Provides realistic metrics to gauge latency and tool use reliability for your streaming RAG agents.

arxiv:2610.35450.title: OBB-PBD: Extending Parallel Box Decoding to Oriented Bounding Boxes for Referring Expression Grounding in Aerial Imagery
arxiv:2610.35450.abstract: Referring expression grounding in overhead imagery requires oriented bounding boxes rather than horizontal ones, since aerial objects appear at arbitrary orientations. Most grounding models emit box coordinates sequentially; Parallel Box Decoding (PBD) instead predicts all geometry slots in one forward pass, but only for four-coordinate horizontal boxes. We extend this block-aligned interface to a six-slot oriented representation using a double-angle parameterization. Rather than assuming correctness from a decreasing loss curve, we verify the extension with image/prompt-shuffle controls and visibility/leakage probes, which show that the corrected model depends on both the image and the prompt rather than on prompt statistics alone. On the aerial vehicle visual grounding (AVVG) benchmark, whose targets are genuinely oriented, the extended model improves rotated intersection over union (rotIoU) from 0.1253 for the zero-shot baseline to 0.303 +/- 0.012 (mean +/- standard deviation over three training seeds) across the complete 6139-record test split spanning all 120 images. Learning oriented boxes rather than their axis-aligned envelopes adds 0.055 +/- 0.008 rotIoU beyond a matched control (per-seed 95% confidence intervals all excluding zero), whereas block expansion alone yields no rotIoU gain distinguishable from zero.
arxiv:2610.35450.summary_hint: The study extends parallel box decoding to oriented bounding boxes via double-angle parameterization, validates it with control probes, and improves rotated IoU on aerial vehicle visual grounding.
arxiv:2610.35450.tldr: Extends Parallel Box Decoding to six‑parameter oriented boxes for aerial referring expression grounding, improving rotIoU from 0.1253 to 0.303 on AVVG benchmark.
arxiv:2610.35450.why: Vision‑specific grounding; not applicable to LLM or RAG systems.

arxiv:2610.34714.title: SearchHorizonBench: A Benchmark for Search Value in AI Agents
arxiv:2610.34714.abstract: AI agents must decide when another search is worth its cost. Answer-success probabilities capture question difficulty, while this decision requires estimating the additional benefit of search. We introduce SearchHorizonBench, a benchmark for learning and evaluating search value from execution experience. Paired continuations and repeated executions separate expected search gain from generation noise and connect prediction quality to decision utility. The resource contains 45,632 executions across 3,168 questions. On 1,632 held-out questions, historical calibration reduces Brier error by 16.2%, with the improvement concentrated in success-level information. Search gains have a standard deviation of 21.4 percentage points, and tested historical estimators explain less than 2% of this variance in point estimates. Matched-configuration learning curves probe this distinction across training scales. At the reference token price, free selection observations yield a 2.49-point utility opportunity over the best constant action, driven primarily by gain information. Reusable histories, frozen splits, strong baselines and scoring tools provide a common foundation for developing and evaluating value-aware search agents.
arxiv:2610.34714.summary_hint: SearchHorizonBench evaluates how agents learn to estimate the value of additional search from execution history, showing that historical calibration improves prediction accuracy but leaves most search-gain variance unexplained.
arxiv:2610.34714.tldr: SearchHorizonBench offers 45,632 executions over 3,168 questions to learn and evaluate the value of additional search; historical calibration cuts Brier error 16.2% and yields 2.49‑point utility gain.
arxiv:2610.34714.why: Helps tune when your RAG system should trigger costly retrieval versus answering directly.

arxiv:2610.34724.title: Harness-Model Collaboration for Long-Horizon Continual Learning
arxiv:2610.34724.abstract: Long-horizon agents continuously encounter reusable procedural knowledge, yet existing systems typically rely either on model adaptation or external memory, trading persistent learning for rapid reuse. This limitation is especially important for Web agents that repeatedly execute related multi-step workflows. We propose HaMo, a Harness-Model collaborative framework that combines fast non-parametric experience accumulation with slow parametric adaptation. HaMo distills trajectories into strategy-level experience cards for immediate retrieval, while an experience-conditioned continual learning objective trains the model to interpret, ground, and execute retrieved strategies across changing contexts. A retrieval-coverage-based selection mechanism further identifies compact and complementary trajectories for parameter updates. Experiments show that HaMo outperforms harness-only and model-only adaptation under within-domain and cross-domain shifts, improving both retention and adaptation. These results highlight the importance of jointly preserving procedural experience and internalizing the competence to transfer and execute it across tasks.
arxiv:2610.34724.summary_hint: HaMo combines rapid retrieval of procedural experience cards with gradual model adaptation to improve long-horizon web agents' retention and cross-task execution.
arxiv:2610.34724.tldr: HaMo combines rapid retrieval of procedural experience cards with gradual model adaptation to improve long-horizon web agents' retention and cross-task execution.

arxiv:2610.37592.title: TANDEM: Balancing Centralized and Decentralized Critics to Address the Information Gap in Complex Multi-Agent Environments
arxiv:2610.37592.abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning under centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) shapes decentralized policies with a centralized critic that observes the global state, then removes the critic at execution. The policies are optimized to rely on information they will not have when they act, an information gap between training and execution. It widens under partial observability, observation noise, and openness, where the set of agents and tasks present changes during an episode. Existing methods transfer centralized guidance in one direction only, removing or distilling the critic once, so the policies never rehearse acting without the critic while they can still be corrected. We propose TANDEM, which keeps one centralized critic and reads it two ways at each training step: a centralized read from the global state, and a decentralized read restricted to the information each agent will have at execution. A parameter-free gate compares the two reads for each agent and trains the policy on the decentralized read where they agree, reinstating the centralized read only where the local view is misleading. A shared target pulls the decentralized read toward the centralized one. We formalize the setting as a task- and agent-open decentralized partially observable Markov decision process (TAO-Dec-POMDP) and evaluate TANDEM on three cooperative domains, each isolating one form of the information gap: discovery for partial observability, sampling for observation noise, and openness in wildfire suppression. We compare against six CTDE baselines and ablate the gate and the shared target; the supplementary material holds the full variant sweep, diagnostics, and learning curves. We measure return at execution, once the centralized critic is removed. TANDEM is the best method on eight of the nine setups and never significantly worse than any baseline.
arxiv:2610.37592.tldr: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning under centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) shapes decentralized policies with a centralized critic that observes the global state, then removes the critic at execution.
arxiv:2610.37592.why: Matches: Agents & orchestration, Evaluation & reliability, Reasoning & post-training

arxiv:2610.36958.title: PailitaoMMSearch2.0 Technical Report: Scaling Generative Retrieval to Unified End-to-End Multimodal Search
arxiv:2610.36958.abstract: Generative retrieval models have been increasingly adopted in search and recommendation systems. However, industrial generative retrieval models are commonly specialized to a fixed online scenario: they learn from scenario-specific interactions, support a narrow set of query forms and retrieval objectives. We study how to remove these couplings and build a unified end-to-end multimodal search system for open-ended image--text queries, heterogeneous shopping intents, and online scenarios with different resource constraints. We present \textbf{PailitaoMMSearch}, which directly generates product Semantic IDs from a raw query image and free-form instruction and scales along three dimensions. \textbf{Data scaling} uses a reusable toolset that can be composed into intent- and lifecycle-specific workflows for cold-start synthesis, quality control, real-traffic refinement, and continuous data production. \textbf{Intent scaling} progressively equips one model with e-commerce product knowledge, multiple retrieval relations, and adjustable reasoning budgets through continual pre-training (CPT), mixed-budget supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and unified reinforcement learning (RL). The RL stage combines intent-balanced optimization and Sample--Beam rollouts aligned with multi-candidate serving. \textbf{Scenario scaling} exposes quality--cost operating points across model capacity and reasoning budget. The system is deployed in multimodal search applications on Taobao Pailitao. A controlled online A/B test reports statistically significant improvements, including item page views $\textbf{+17.90\%}$, transactions $\textbf{+27.04\%}$, and gross merchandise value $\textbf{+8.94\%}$.
arxiv:2610.36958.tldr: They built PailitaoMMSearch, a unified multimodal generative retrieval system that generates product IDs from images and text, scaling via data pipelines and continual pre‑training across intents.
arxiv:2610.36958.why: Shows how to scale generative retrieval across modalities and intents, offering patterns for building unified RAG pipelines in production.

arxiv:2610.36389.title: MAREval: A Multi-Agent Framework for Evaluating Natural Language Recommendation Explanations
arxiv:2610.36389.abstract: Evaluating natural language explanations in recommender systems is essential for fostering user trust, transparency, and engagement. However, existing evaluation approaches like human evaluations, while accurate, are resource-intensive and impractical at the scale required by modern recommendation platforms. Also, automated methods using single-agent LLMs suffer from prompt sensitivity and inconsistent outputs. To address these challenges, we propose MAREval, a structured multi-agent framework for evaluating recommendation explanations using large language models. MAREval orchestrates (i) a planner agent that uses a novel Chain of Debate (CoD) prompting strategy to coordinate agent roles and enforce logically consistent evaluation plans; (ii) a moderator agent that regulates discussions by mitigating prompt drift; and (iii) an arbitrator agent that aggregates outputs from multiple evaluation rounds and (iv) a Monte Carlo sampling method, improving robustness and alignment with human judgment. We conduct comprehensive evaluations on both public (TopicalChat) and proprietary recommendation datasets, demonstrating that MAREval outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Comprehensive experiments on a public benchmark and a proprietary e-commerce dataset show that MAREval improves alignment with human judgments over strong singleand multi-agent baselines. Stability analyses indicate substantially lower variability across repeated trials. In a large human-annotation gate, MAREval meets production quality thresholds where prior evaluators fall short, and online A/B testing demonstrates statistically significant improvements in engagement and revenue metrics. These results establish MAREval as a scalable and reliable solution for human-aligned evaluation of recommendation explanations in real-world systems
arxiv:2610.36389.tldr: MAREval orchestrates planner, moderator, and arbitrator agents with Chain‑of‑Debate prompting and Monte‑Carlo sampling to produce robust, human‑aligned evaluation of recommendation explanations.
arxiv:2610.36389.why: Provides a structured multi‑agent evaluation pipeline that can be adapted for LLM app testing.

arxiv:2610.36383.title: From Generation to Scoring: Scaling LLM-Based Semantic Labeling at LinkedIn
arxiv:2610.36383.abstract: For efficiency, industrial large language model (LLM) labelers often pack many candidate labels into one prompt and generate a YES/NO answer for each, even when each decision depends only on the entity and one candidate. Generating these independent decisions as one answer list couples them, spends decoding on the list, and relies on the list being well-formed. In this paper, we present an end-to-end recipe that reformulates the labeler as semantic scoring, fine-tuning it on single-candidate prompts to return each decision as one answer-token score from a prefill-only pass. We also adapt Multiple-Item Scoring (MIS) to score hundreds of candidates in one sequence with attention masked between them. Deployed for profile qualification labeling at LinkedIn, semantic scoring changes at most 0.01% of decisions when candidates are reordered and matches the agreement with reference labels that packed generation reaches only with about 4.7x as many training pairs. The MIS-based stack raises throughput over the deployed stack by 1.24x offline and 1.9x in model serving under a one-second p99 latency target. For offline batch inference, we implement MIS-based scoring as a reusable, model-agnostic Ray Data API proposed for upstream adoption. Model serving uses MIS support contributed to SGLang.
arxiv:2610.36383.tldr: They replace multi‑label generation with single‑candidate semantic scoring, using masked attention to score hundreds of candidates, cutting latency 1.9× while preserving accuracy.
arxiv:2610.36383.why: Directly applicable method to speed up LLM‑based classification or retrieval scoring in production pipelines.

arxiv:2610.36221.title: EREBOTS 4.0: A framework for conversational assistants with A2A agents and MCP tools
arxiv:2610.36221.abstract: In recent years, multi-agent systems have shifted from rule-based, symbolic agents to sub-symbolic agents built on language models. However, several limitations remain unresolved. The new frontier is neuro-symbolic agents, which pair language models with deterministic tools and explicit protocols. Without a common framework to standardize and compose them, each study rebuilds the same infrastructure, and results are hard to replicate. This paper presents EREBOTS 4.0, an open-source, hybrid-AI, multi-agent framework that fills this gap for conversational assistants. Language-model agents plan and route requests, while deterministic tools compute exact results over the Model Context Protocol (MCP). An orchestrator selects one or more specialist agents per turn and calls them over the Agent2Agent protocol (A2A). A new agent, local or remote, is added by listing its URL in a configuration file. The framework also manages identity, user context with consent flags, task states and traces. Its A2A server passed 97 tracked requirements in the official A2A Technology Compatibility Kit, with no failures.
arxiv:2610.36221.tldr: EREBOTS 4.0 offers an open‑source hybrid‑AI multi‑agent framework where language‑model agents plan, deterministic tools compute, and an orchestrator routes requests via standardized A2A and MCP protocols.
arxiv:2610.36221.why: Provides reusable infrastructure for building reliable multi‑agent LLM assistants, accelerating internal development.

arxiv:2610.35542.title: Hypergraph-Enhanced Evidence Selection for Long-Context Multimodal Document QA
arxiv:2610.35542.abstract: Long-context multimodal document question answering (QA) has become an important yet challenging task for modern vision-language models (VLMs), as it requires reasoning over evidence dispersed across pages and modalities within limited input budgets. Current pipelines adopt retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to select multimodal evidence for downstream VLMs. However, existing systems mainly rely on static selection rules over fixed-granularity retrieval units such as pages or blocks, resulting in information loss during retrieval and suboptimal performance in downstream reasoning. To alleviate these issues, we formulate the core task as budget-aware evidence selection over structured document evidence and propose HyperDoc, a document RAG framework that constructs compact yet sufficient evidence while preserving document relations. Specifically, HyperDoc constructs a document hypergraph to explicitly capture structural, logical, and cross-modal relationships among multimodal document elements. Over this structured evidence space, HyperDoc performs adaptive cost-aware hyperedge selection based on query intent and input budget. Extensive experiments on three representative benchmarks demonstrate that HyperDoc outperforms various types of state-of-the-art baselines.
arxiv:2610.35542.tldr: HyperDoc builds a hypergraph of multimodal document elements and selects cost‑aware hyperedges to create compact evidence sets, improving QA performance under limited context budgets.
arxiv:2610.35542.why: Offers a budget‑aware evidence selection technique to boost multimodal RAG effectiveness in document‑heavy applications.

arxiv:2610.35398.title: Belief-Conditioned Multi-Agent Actor Critic for Decentralized LLM Collaboration
arxiv:2610.35398.abstract: Recent work has explored optimizing LLM collaboration through Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), but many approaches still rely on predefined workflows, limiting efficiency and scalability. Decentralized LLM collaboration is challenging because agents execute independently with limited communication, share a joint objective, and must infer useful information from communication traces. In this paper, we propose BCMAAC, a Belief-Conditioned Multi-Agent Actor-Critic method that maintains beliefs over contextual information and uses them to facilitate training. Experiments on Minecraft game-playing, web searching and tool-using tasks show that BCMAAC improves task performance and collaborative behavior compared to naive actor-critic baselines. The improvements are particularly pronounced in multi-turn tasks with richer contextual information, where belief modeling provides a clear advantage.
arxiv:2610.35398.tldr: BCMAAC introduces belief‑conditioned actor‑critic training for decentralized LLM agents, improving collaborative task performance in web‑search and tool‑use benchmarks.
arxiv:2610.35398.why: Shows advanced MARL training that may inform future agent coordination, but not ready for immediate production use.

arxiv:2610.35240.title: Reading Beyond OCR Noise: Robust Cross-Lingual RAG for Legislative Archives
